'''Tapirapé''' (also known as '''Apyãwa''' and '''Tapi'irape''') is a [[Tupi–Guarani languages|Tupí-Guaraní]] language of [[Brazil]] spoken near the [[Araguaia River]], in the border of the states of [[Mato Grosso]] and [[Tocantins]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rodrigues |first=Aryon Dall’Igna |date=2011 |title=Relações internas na família linguística Tupí-Guaraní |url=https://periodicos.unb.br/index.php/ling/article/view/16264 |journal=Revista Brasileira de Linguística Antropológica |language=pt |volume=3 |issue=2 |doi=10.26512/rbla.v3i2.16264 |issn=2317-1375|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>DIETRICH, Wolf. O tronco tupi e as suas famílias de línguas. Classificação e esboço tipológico. In: NOLL, Volker. ''O Português e o Tupi no Brasil''. São Paulo: Editora Contexto, 2010.</ref> As of 2020, the language has around 917 speakers,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Quadro Geral dos Povos - Povos Indígenas no Brasil |url=https://www.indios.org.br/pt/Quadro_Geral_dos_Povos |access-date=2024-05-25 |website=www.indios.org.br}}</ref> who belong to the [[Tapirapé]] ethnic group.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Quadro Geral dos Povos - Povos Indígenas no Brasil |url=https://www.indios.org.br/pt/Quadro_Geral_dos_Povos |access-date=2024-05-25 |website=www.indios.org.br}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The term "Tapirapé", originated in [[Tupi language|Tupi]], means "[[tapir]]'s way" (''tapi'ira'', tapir + ''apé'', way.) This was the way that the ancestral indigenous people called the [[Milky Way]], and it was the name given to the people by the foreigners (mãira.) Even though this was not how these indigenous people called themselves (apyãwa,) the term began to be used by them as a way to identify their language and themselves, both in [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]] and in the Tapirapé language.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Morfossintaxe da língua Tapirapé (Praça 2007) - Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendajú |url=http://etnolinguistica.wikidot.com/tese:praca-2007 |access-date=2024-05-25 |website=etnolinguistica.wikidot.com}}</ref>

==Language contact==
Ribeiro (2012) finds a number of Apyãwa loanwords in [[Karajá language|Karajá]] (such as ''bèhyra'' 'carrying basket', ''kòmỹdawyra'' {{'}}''andu'' beans', ''hãrara'' 'macaw (sp.)', ''tarawè'' 'parakeet (sp.)', ''txakohi'' 'Txakohi ceremonial mask', ''hyty'' 'garbage (Javaé dialect)') as well as several Karajá loans in Apyãwa (''tãtã'' 'banana', ''tori'' 'White man', ''marara'' 'turtle stew', ''irãwore'' 'Irabure ceremonial mask'). Some of the latter loans are also found in other Tupí-Guaraní languages closely related to Apyãwa, such as [[Parakanã language|Parakanã]] and [[Asuriní of Trocará language|Asuriní of Trocará]] (''sata'' 'banana', ''toria'' 'White man').<ref>{{cite thesis|last=Ribeiro |first=Eduardo Rivail |date=2012 |title=A grammar of Karajá |type=Ph.D. dissertation |location=Chicago |publisher=University of Chicago}}</ref>{{rp|10–2}}

==Phonology==
The phonology of the Tapirapé language originated in the [[Proto-Tupian language]]. Among its main features, the presence of [[Alternation (linguistics)|alternation]] and [[Nasal vowel|vowel nasality]] processes stand out.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A língua Tapirapé (Almeida, Irmãzinhas de Jesus & Paula 1983) - Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendajú |url=http://www.etnolinguistica.org/biblio:almeida-1983-tapirape |access-date=2024-05-25 |website=www.etnolinguistica.org}}</ref>

=== Vowels ===
Differently from most Tupian languages, the Tapirapé people make use of five vowel phonemes, going against the predominant six vowel system in the family.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |title=Aspectos da fonologia e morfofonologia Tapirapé (Leite 1977) - Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendajú |url=http://www.etnolinguistica.org/biblio:leite-1977-aspectos |access-date=2024-05-25 |website=www.etnolinguistica.org}}</ref> All five vowels have five nasal counterparts.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Estrutura silábica e articulação secundária em tapirapé (Leite 1995) - Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendajú |url=http://www.etnolinguistica.org/biblio:leite-1995-estrutura |access-date=2024-05-25 |website=www.etnolinguistica.org}}</ref>

* The vowel /[[Close central unrounded vowel|ɨ]]/ is, most of the time, realised as a close central unrounded vowel. Due to the variation in the height of the tongue in the emission of vowel phonemes, this representation also includes the phoneme [<nowiki/>[[Mid central vowel|ə]]], which only differs from /[[Close central unrounded vowel|ɨ]]/ in its height.
* The phoneme /e/ represents both [<nowiki/>[[Mid front unrounded vowel|e̞]]] and [<nowiki/>[[Open-mid front unrounded vowel|ɛ]]], depending on the height variation of the tongue in one's mouth.
* The vowel /[[Close front unrounded vowel|i]]/ is realised as a close front unrounded vowel.
* Unlike other vowel phonemes, the nature of the vowel /o/ is controversial; it is seen as an interpretation of the vowel {{IPAlink|u}}, [{{IPAlink|o}}], and {{IPAlink|ɔ}}, all of which are rounded and back vowels. The use of the phoneme /{{IPAlink|o}}/ as a representative of this set is influenced by the vowel evolution of [[Asuriní language|Asuríni]], a similar language, where the Proto-Tupian phoneme [{{IPAlink|u}}] was neutralised into [{{IPAlink|o}}].<ref name=":02" />

* Yonne Leite, in his article about the syllabic structure of Tapirapé, mentions that /j/ has five possible allophones: [<nowiki/>[[Voiceless postalveolar affricate|tʃ]]], [<nowiki/>[[Palatalization (phonetics)|tʲ]]], [<nowiki/>[[Voiceless palatal nasal|ɲ]]], and [<nowiki/>[[Nasal palatal approximant|j̃]]]. He says that, in onsets, [tʲ] and [tʃ] appear frequently, while [j] appears in codas and in onsets of posttonic syllables when, in the nucleus of the syllable, the vowel is oral. The palatal nasal and the nasal palatal approximant appear in the codas of a tonic syllable and in the onset of a posttonic syllable when, in the nucleus of the syllable, the vowel is nasal.<ref name=":0" />
